title: Online shop — from checkout to dispatch
subtitle: How an order gets out of the door today, and what same-day dispatch would change
source: Illustrative example for the blog post *Understanding Is the New Bottleneck*. Not a real client.
summary: A customer checks out in the **shop**. The order waits there until a **nightly sync** sends it to the **warehouse system**. The warehouse then picks, packs and ships it, or turns it into a **back-order** if a SKU is out of stock.

summary.title: The one idea to keep
summary.text: Orders reach the warehouse once a night. Every promise about dispatch time is limited by that one step, not by how fast the warehouse works.

sections.title: Glossary
sections.summary: Three teams, three names for the same thing.

head: Term
Meaning
Watch out
rows: What a customer buys in one checkout.
One product variant the warehouse stocks.
One T-shirt in three sizes is three SKUs.
An accepted order for something out of stock.
The customer has paid; nothing ships yet.

sections.title: Today: checkout to dispatch
sections.summary: Orders move to the warehouse in one batch, overnight.
blocks: The shop saves each order as **Placed**. At 02:00 the nightly sync sends every Placed order to the warehouse system.
In the morning the warehouse picks and packs. If every SKU is in stock, the order ships. If not, it becomes a back-order and the customer gets an email.

blocks.text: Orders placed after 02:00 wait almost a full day before the warehouse sees them.

sections.title: Target: same-day dispatch
sections.summary: Orders placed before 14:00 should leave the same day.
blocks: The business wants same-day dispatch for orders placed before 14:00.

blocks.text: Whether back-orders are part of the same-day promise is not decided. See [[questions:backorder_promise]].

sections.title: The gap
sections.summary: The nightly sync, not the warehouse, blocks same-day dispatch.
blocks: Same-day dispatch needs orders to reach the warehouse within minutes. That means a **real-time order feed**, not a faster warehouse team.

walkthroughs.title: Follow one order: Maya's T-shirt
walkthroughs.intro: An example case; the rules come from the process above. Maya buys a blue T-shirt in size M at 13:40 on a Tuesday.

steps.title: Maya checks out
blocks: She pays, and the shop saves her order as Placed.

steps.title: When does the warehouse see it?
blocks: She ordered at 13:40, before the 14:00 cut-off the business wants.

choices.label: Within minutes, so it can leave today

steps.title: Not today
blocks: Today the shop only sends orders in the nightly sync. The 14:00 cut-off is the *target*, not how it works now.

steps.title: The nightly sync sends it
blocks: At 02:00 the order reaches the warehouse system, about twelve hours after she paid.

steps.title: The warehouse picks it
blocks: The blue M is in stock, even though the blue L is not.

choices.label: It ships: stock is checked per SKU
It becomes a back-order: the product is partly out of stock

steps.title: Not a back-order
blocks: Stock is checked per **SKU**. Blue L being out of stock doesn't affect blue M.

steps.title: It ships on Wednesday
blocks: Maya's order leaves a day later than the business wants. Same-day dispatch needs the [[map:sync|real-time feed]].

questions.title: Are back-orders part of the same-day promise?
blocks: If yes, partial shipments may be needed. If no, the promise only covers in-stock orders.

questions.title: Is 14:00 the cut-off at weekends too?
Who owns the real-time feed if the warehouse system is down?
blocks: Orders need somewhere to wait without being lost.

choices: Orders only reach the warehouse in the nightly sync
explain: The warehouse can't pick an order it hasn't received. The nightly sync, not picking speed, sets the delay.

quiz.q: Blue L is out of stock. Maya orders blue M. What happens?
explain: Stock is checked per **SKU**, not per product. Blue M is its own SKU.

quiz.q: Finance talks about a *sale* and the warehouse about a *shipment*. What are they?
choices: The same Order under different names
A sale is an order that has shipped
explain: Same thing, three names. Pick one term (**Order**) and use it everywhere.

quiz.q: A customer has a back-order. Have they paid?
explain: Payment is taken at checkout. A back-order is a paid order waiting for stock.

quiz.q: What does same-day dispatch need first?
quiz.answer: A real-time order feed from the shop to the warehouse.
